A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the early ERP response to another’s distress is a non-empathy component, and the later ERP component is an empathic component that is differentially modulated in psychopathy.
psychopathic individuals have a specific electrophysiological impairment in empathic concern that is not present in the automatic affective sharing response.
psychopathy is associated with an attenuated neural response to the distress cues of another person, but only in the context of empathic concern.
The main takeaway from our work is that
affective sharing and the cognitive-affective differentiation of empathic concern are distinct processes that may be differentially impacted in psychopathy.
the neural signatures of empathic concern are distinct from those of affective sharing, and that psychopathic traits are associated with impairments in both of these components of empathy.
psychopathy is a multidimensional construct that is not reducible to a unitary neural signature, and that it may be possible to disentangle its components at a neurophysiological level.
